checkpoints.title: Until DNS Returns the Record Corresponding to the Domain Name
checkpoints.prompt: A network administrator is investigating why internal.example.com cannot be resolved by an EC2 instance in the VPC. Select one piece of information to check first.

choices.text: Check the association between the querying VPC and the private hosted zone, and check the record name
choices.explanation: This verifies the Resolver's lookup scope and the target name.

choices.text: Reissue the certificate
choices.explanation: This is not directly related to the problem before DNS resolution.

choices.text: Set the TTL to 0
choices.explanation: This does not fix a missing association or record.

choices.text: Unconditionally add the same record to the public zone
choices.explanation: This changes the design boundary for the private name.

learning.reason: This verifies the Resolver's lookup scope and the target name.

checkpoints.title: Choose the DNS record that matches the destination
checkpoints.prompt: A DNS administrator directs example.com, the apex of a Route 53 hosted zone, to a CloudFront distribution. Choose one record configuration to use.

choices.text: CNAME
choices.explanation: You cannot create a CNAME record at the zone apex.

choices.text: MX
choices.explanation: For mail delivery destinations.

choices.text: Alias A or Alias AAAA record
choices.explanation: It can direct traffic to a supported AWS resource by alias.

choices.text: TXT
choices.explanation: It is not used to specify a destination with arbitrary text.

learning.reason: It can direct traffic to a supported AWS resource by alias.

checkpoints.title: TTL is the time a cache can retain a response
checkpoints.prompt: After a DNS administrator switches the destination, some users are still connecting to the old IP address. Choose one reason why shortening the TTL at this point does not make the old response disappear immediately.

choices.text: Route 53 is rejecting the change
choices.explanation: It does not necessarily mean that the change was rejected.

choices.text: The resolver is caching the existing response according to the old TTL
choices.explanation: Existing caches remain until the old TTL expires.

choices.text: A records cannot be changed
choices.explanation: A records can also be changed.

choices.text: The TLS certificate fixes DNS
choices.explanation: TLS and DNS caching are separate.

source.label: Route 53 DNS settings not in effect

learning.reason: Existing caches remain until the old TTL expires.

checkpoints.title: Troubleshoot name resolution and post-connection failures
checkpoints.prompt: An operations engineer confirmed with dig that the order site resolves to the expected IP address. The browser displays a certificate error over the HTTPS connection. Choose one next troubleshooting step.

choices.text: Delete the DNS record
choices.explanation: This breaks name resolution.

choices.text: Shorten the TTL
choices.explanation: This does not fix the existing certificate error.

choices.text: Stop Route 53
choices.explanation: This does not isolate a problem outside DNS.

choices.text: Check the name, validity period, and TLS settings of the certificate presented by the destination
choices.explanation: This verifies the TLS responsibility after DNS succeeds.

learning.reason: This verifies the TLS responsibility after DNS succeeds.

choices.text: Return connection destination information corresponding to a name
choices.explanation: DNS returns record responses based on names.

choices.text: Guarantee the validity of HTTPS certificates
choices.explanation: Verification of TLS certificates is separate from DNS.

choices.text: Complete application authentication
choices.explanation: Authentication is the responsibility of the application.

finalQuestions.prompt: When a user connects to www.example.com, select two incorrect statements about the role of DNS.
finalQuestions.title: The role of name resolution

choices.text: Allow the private hosted zone to be resolved from the entire Internet
choices.explanation: A private hosted zone is used for name resolution within the VPCs associated with it.

choices.text: Verify the association between the querying VPC and the private hosted zone, as well as the record name
choices.explanation: You can verify the zone and name that Resolver can reference.

choices.text: Write IP addresses in every configuration without using DNS
choices.explanation: This makes operational changes and troubleshooting difficult.

finalQuestions.prompt: A network administrator is evaluating a configuration that allows names registered in a Route 53 private hosted zone to be resolved from EC2 instances within a VPC. Select two of the following configurations that are incorrect.
finalQuestions.title: VPC Name Resolution

choices.text: An A record for an IPv4 address
choices.explanation: An A record maps to IPv4.

choices.text: An AAAA record for an IPv6 address
choices.explanation: An AAAA record maps to IPv6.

choices.text: Only an MX record for the mail delivery destination
choices.explanation: MX is for a mail delivery destination, not a Web address.

finalQuestions.prompt: Make web.example.com reachable over both IPv4 and IPv6. Select two combinations of records that are required.
finalQuestions.title: A and AAAA

choices.text: Create a CNAME record at the hosted zone apex that points to the CloudFront domain name.
choices.explanation: A standard CNAME record cannot be created at the hosted zone apex. Use an alias when pointing to CloudFront.

choices.text: For IPv4, create an alias A record that points to the CloudFront distribution.
choices.explanation: A Route 53 alias A record can point from the hosted zone apex to CloudFront.

choices.text: For IPv6, create an alias AAAA record that points to the CloudFront distribution.
choices.explanation: When IPv6 is also provided, configure an alias AAAA record separately from the A record.

finalQuestions.prompt: A DNS administrator directs the apex of the hosted zone, example.com, to an IPv6-enabled CloudFront distribution. The alternate domain name and certificate are already configured on the distribution. Select one incorrect Route 53 configuration.
finalQuestions.title: Aliases and CNAME

choices.text: CNAME record
choices.explanation: CNAME points to another DNS name.

choices.text: AAAA record
choices.explanation: AAAA points to an IPv6 address.

choices.text: CAA record
choices.explanation: CAA is used to control certificate issuers.

finalQuestions.prompt: A DNS administrator wants the subdomain api.example.com to be an alias for api.vendor.example.net, which is managed by another provider. Select one DNS record to use for this purpose.
finalQuestions.title: Record types

choices.text: Set the TTL to 0 and issue the certificate
choices.explanation: TTL does not fix a certificate name mismatch.

choices.text: Check the name and expiration date of the certificate at the destination, along with the CloudFront-side settings
choices.explanation: This lets you investigate DNS and TLS responsibilities separately.

choices.text: Change the A record to an MX record
choices.explanation: A mail record does not resolve a certificate problem.

finalQuestions.prompt: A web administrator confirmed that the website name resolves to the intended CloudFront distribution, but the browser displays an HTTPS certificate error. Select one setting to check next.
finalQuestions.title: Records and TLS

choices.text: The resolver may be caching the old response according to the old TTL
choices.explanation: Existing caches remain until the old TTL expires.

choices.text: A DNS change is always reflected immediately for all users
choices.explanation: This ignores the resolver's cache.

choices.text: Changing the TTL immediately deletes existing caches
choices.explanation: The TTL after the change does not clear existing caches.

finalQuestions.prompt: A DNS administrator changed the destination IP address for api.example.com. The authoritative DNS returns the new value, but some users still connect to the old IP address. Select one possible reason.

source.label: Route 53 DNS settings not in effect

finalQuestions.title: TTL and propagation

choices.text: Shorten only the TTL immediately after the cutover.
choices.explanation: Caches using the old TTL remain.

choices.text: Continue running the old destination until caches of old DNS responses expire after the cutover.
choices.explanation: This allows users using old responses to continue connecting.

choices.text: Check the current TTL before the cutover, shorten the TTL, and then wait until caches obtained with the previous longer TTL expire.
choices.explanation: Shortening the TTL first does not immediately change the expiration time of caches stored with the old TTL.

finalQuestions.prompt: An operations team for an online sales site will change the Route 53 DNS record the next day to switch the destination. They want users who are still using old DNS responses to be able to continue connecting. Choose two correct cutover plans.
finalQuestions.title: TTL Before Cutover

choices.text: Route 53 receives 300 queries.
choices.explanation: TTL is not a count.

choices.text: The resolver can normally cache the response for up to 300 seconds.
choices.explanation: TTL indicates the cache duration in seconds.

choices.text: It is a different value from the HTTP response time.
choices.explanation: TTL indicates the cache duration of a DNS response.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose one incorrect statement about what DNS record TTL=300 indicates.
finalQuestions.title: Meaning of TTL

choices.text: Review the CloudFront origin settings to verify that the destination hostname, protocol, and port are correct.
choices.explanation: Because the request reached CloudFront from the viewer, investigate the connection conditions from CloudFront to the origin.

choices.text: Recreate the DNS record used by viewers and do not investigate communication from CloudFront to the origin.
choices.explanation: The name used by viewers has already resolved successfully. To investigate the cause of the 502, check the responses from CloudFront and the origin.

choices.text: Record the time of occurrence and the request identifier, then compare the CloudFront response with the origin-side records.
choices.explanation: Following the record for the relevant request helps narrow down whether it reached the destination and which side returned the response.

finalQuestions.prompt: A web operations staff member confirmed that the hostname of an order site resolves to CloudFront as expected. The browser receives HTTP 502 from CloudFront. Choose one incorrect investigation approach at this stage.
finalQuestions.title: DNS and HTTP

choices.text: Treat TLS as healthy because DNS is healthy
choices.explanation: DNS responses and certificate validation are separate.

choices.text: Check the health check request content and monitoring conditions
choices.explanation: Identify what the health check is checking.

choices.text: Check the health check conditions and the certificate name, expiration, and TLS settings separately
choices.explanation: This separates the responsibilities of monitoring and TLS.

finalQuestions.prompt: Even though the Route 53 health check is healthy, users are receiving TLS errors. Select two things that should be checked.
finalQuestions.title: Health Check Scope

choices.text: Expose the private zone to the entire internet
choices.explanation: This contradicts the purpose of a private zone.

choices.text: Maintain a public zone for external users
choices.explanation: Name resolution for external users can continue.

choices.text: Assign a fixed IP to every client
choices.explanation: This loses the management provided by name resolution.

choices.text: Verify the private hosted zone's VPC association and the expected responses inside and outside the VPC
choices.explanation: This allows the query scope to be separated in the design.

finalQuestions.prompt: There are public and private hosted zones with the same name, and you want to return a different destination only inside the VPC. Select two incorrect designs.
finalQuestions.title: Public Boundary

blocks.label: Overview
blocks.text: Evaluate name resolution, record types, TTL, and TLS and HTTP after DNS as separate responsibilities.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Choose the query scope and records, estimate the caching impact of TTL, and distinguish connections and TLS after DNS.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Explain the query scope of public hosted zones, private hosted zones, and resolvers.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Choose A/AAAA, CNAME, and alias records based on destination and naming constraints.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Plan DNS cutovers while considering TTL and existing caches.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Separate the responsibilities of DNS, TLS, HTTP, and health checks to troubleshoot failures.

blocks.label: Until DNS returns the record corresponding to the domain name
blocks.text: DNS queries the record corresponding to a domain name so that the user can obtain the destination. In Route 53 public hosted zones and private hosted zones, the scope reached by queries differs.

blocks.label: Until DNS returns the record corresponding to the domain name
blocks.text: For name resolution within a VPC, use Amazon Route 53 VPC Resolver. It resolves VPC-specific names and records in private hosted zones, and also handles queries to public DNS. If name resolution fails, check the query source, hosted zone, DNS delegation, and target record in that order.

blocks.label: Until DNS returns the record corresponding to the domain name
blocks.text: A DNS response provides information about the destination. Even after receiving a response, the HTTP response, TLS certificate, and application authorization may not all succeed.

steps.label: Until DNS returns the record corresponding to the domain name

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: An EC2 instance in a VPC cannot resolve api.example.com.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Identify the resolver and VPC queried by the EC2 instance.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Check the private hosted zone association and record name.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Use dig or a similar tool to verify the response, and separately verify TCP/TLS after DNS.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can investigate DNS problems separately from connection and TLS problems.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If a DNS name resolves to an IP address, the web application will always be usable.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: DNS only returns the connection endpoint. Check HTTP, TLS, security groups, and application authentication separately.

blocks.label: Key Points
blocks.text: Check the scope of the resolver and hosted zone.

blocks.label: Key Points
blocks.text: Verify name resolution and application connectivity separately.

blocks.label: Key Points
blocks.text: Be aware of the query scope of public DNS and VPC DNS.

blocks.label: Choose the DNS Record That Matches the Destination
blocks.text: An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address, while an AAAA record maps a name to an IPv6 address. A CNAME points to another DNS name, and a Route 53 alias record can be used to direct a name to a supported AWS resource.

blocks.label: Choose the DNS Record That Matches the Destination
blocks.text: Match the record type to the form of the destination and the name being queried. Also check the restriction that prevents a CNAME from being placed at the zone apex and the restrictions on the AWS resources that can be specified by an alias record.

blocks.label: Choose the DNS Record That Matches the Destination
blocks.text: TXT, MX, and CAA records serve purposes other than web destinations. When troubleshooting name resolution, compare the expected record type with the actual response.

steps.label: Choose the DNS Record That Matches the Destination

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: Point www.example.com to CloudFront.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Check CloudFront's DNS name and whether it is the zone apex.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: In Route 53, select the corresponding alias A/AAAA record.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Check the response with dig, and also check the TLS settings on the CloudFront side.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can configure the mapping between the AWS resource and the name with a record that meets the restrictions.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If it is an AWS resource, you can place a CNAME on any name.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Check the zone apex restrictions and the mapping to the AWS resource, and select an alias A/AAAA record when necessary.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Distinguish the meanings of A/AAAA, CNAME, and alias records.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Check the zone apex and resource constraints.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Check DNS records and TLS settings separately.

blocks.label: TTL is how long a cache can retain a response
blocks.text: TTL is the number of seconds a DNS resolver can retain a record response in its cache. Even after a record is changed, an existing cache may continue returning the old value until the previous TTL expires.

blocks.label: TTL is how long a cache can retain a response
blocks.text: Changing the TTL to a shorter value during incident response does not immediately remove values that have already been cached. Plan the TTL before the switchover and operate on the assumption that some users will still receive the old value during the transition.

blocks.label: TTL is how long a cache can retain a response
blocks.text: For alias records, the TTL may be determined by the target AWS resource. Do not confuse the time required for a record change to propagate with the change having reached Route 53.

steps.label: TTL is how long a cache can retain a response

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: During incident response, switch api.example.com to a new load balancer.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Check the current TTL and the possible remaining cache duration.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Decide the switching criteria and how long to maintain the old destination.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: After the switchover, observe responses and application status from multiple resolvers.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can design the switchover and monitoring while accounting for how long old responses remain.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If you shorten the TTL immediately after changing the record, all users will see the new value.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Existing caches remain until the old TTL expires. Plan the TTL and waiting time before the switch.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: TTL is the resolver's cache duration.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Switch over on the assumption that old responses will remain after a change.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Also verify how the TTL of an alias record is determined.

blocks.label: Distinguishing name-resolution failures from post-connection failures
blocks.text: DNS returns a destination from a name. Whether a TCP connection can be established to the returned destination, whether HTTP returns the expected response, and whether the TLS certificate matches the name are separate checks.

blocks.label: Distinguishing name-resolution failures from post-connection failures
blocks.text: Route 53 health checks and routing policies affect the selection of DNS responses, but they do not guarantee that all application functions are working correctly. Make the monitoring targets and switchover conditions explicit.

blocks.label: Distinguishing name-resolution failures from post-connection failures
blocks.text: Diagram the owners of public DNS, private hosted zones, load balancers, CloudFront, and certificates to identify which layer is failing.

steps.label: Distinguishing name-resolution failures from post-connection failures

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: DNS is correct, but the user sees a certificate error over HTTPS.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Use dig to check the name and response.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Check the name and expiration date of the certificate presented by the destination.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Record HTTP responses, TLS, and DNS as separate monitoring items.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Do not mistake successful DNS for successful TLS or the application.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If the Route 53 health check is healthy, the HTTPS certificate must also be correct.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: The health-check conditions and certificate validation are separate. Check the DNS, TLS, and HTTP responses individually.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: DNS is the entry point that returns the destination.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: TLS certificates and HTTP responses have separate responsibilities.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Make the monitoring and failover conditions explicit.
